props.title: Grindhouse

sections.content: **Grindhouse (2007)** (2007) represents the ultimate love letter to 1970s exploitation cinema from directors Quentin Tarantino and Robert Rodriguez. This ambitious double feature recreates the grimy theater experience complete with fake trailers, film damage, and missing reels. Rodriguez's Planet Terror (2007) delivers zombie mayhem and machine gun prosthetics, while Tarantino's Death Proof (2007) transforms the muscle car movies of the 70s into a feminist revenge thriller. The project follows in the tradition of drive-in classics like **I Drink Your Blood** (1970) and **Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill!** (1965).

movies.title: Machete
movies.slug: Danny Trejo's fake trailer character gets his own full exploitation feature about a betrayed federale seeking revenge

sections.content: The fake trailers between features became legendary in their own right. Machete (2010) expanded into two full features. Edgar Wright's "Don't" perfectly captured British horror aesthetics. Rob Zombie's "Werewolf Women of the SS" and Eli Roth's "Thanksgiving" showed how well modern directors understood exploitation tropes. These shorts connect to a rich history of exploitation film marketing, where outrageous trailers often outshined the actual movies. SUBHEAD: The Exploitation Revival Wave

**Grindhouse** sparked renewed interest in exploitation cinema, influencing films like **Hobo with a Shotgun** (2011), **Black Dynamite** (2009), and **Drive Angry** (2011). These modern takes balanced homage with self-awareness, celebrating the excesses of their inspiration while adding contemporary production values and social commentary. The movement peaked with **Machete Kills** (2013) before largely moving to streaming platforms where exploitation-style films found new audiences.
